title: Japan Signals the Free Ride Is Over With Record Defense Spending Surge
excerpt: Under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Tokyo has boosted military spending past $58 billion, expanded arms exports, and signaled willingness to fight over Taiwan — fundamentally reshaping the U.S. alliance and alarming Beijing.
body:
• Japan has increased defense spending more than 9% this year to approximately 9 trillion yen ($58 billion) under PM Sanae Takaichi, with a pledge to reach 2% of GDP — and U.S. officials are pushing for 2.5% or higher.
  • Japan's Self-Defense Forces fired their first missiles outside Japanese territorial waters in joint drills, and Tokyo has begun selling warships to the Philippines and Australia.
  • Takaichi has called a Chinese attack on Taiwan an "existential threat" to Japan, prompting Beijing to cancel airline flights, ban critical mineral exports, and issue sharp warnings.
  • A February election supermajority gives Takaichi the votes to potentially amend Japan's pacifist post-war constitution for the first time.

When the U.S. minesweeper Vigilance — launched in Seattle in 1943 and transferred to the Philippines in 1967 — was finally sunk last month in joint drills, it was destroyed by the first missiles Japan's post-war military has ever fired outside its own territorial waters. The symbolism was hard to miss.

Under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Japan is undergoing the most dramatic military transformation since the end of World War II. Defense spending has jumped more than 9% this year to roughly 9 trillion yen ($58 billion), with a commitment to double arms spending to 2% of gross domestic product over five years. U.S. officials want even more.

Washington's Expectations Keep Rising

At the Shangri-La security dialogue in Singapore, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth praised Japan's "interests-based" approach, contrasting it favorably with what he called the "drama and moralising" of European allies. But he made clear that the bar keeps moving.

https://x.com/ChinaMilBugle/status/2088516418132386232

"We have high expectations of our Japanese allies, and together we can and must each pull our weight."

— U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Shangri-La Dialogue

Other U.S. officials have urged Japan to move to at least 2.5% of GDP, in line with expectations Washington has set for NATO members and other allies. The message is unmistakable: America wants Japan to shoulder more of the Pacific defense burden, and Tokyo appears willing.

Taiwan at the Center

It is Japan's posture on Taiwan that has most alarmed Beijing. Shortly after taking office, Takaichi declared that any Chinese attempt to overrun Taiwan would constitute an "existential threat" to Japan — language that implies Tokyo might use force under security laws passed in 2015 that allow military action in "survival-threatening situations" even without a direct attack.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi called the remarks "shocking." Beijing's UN ambassador labeled them a "threat of force" violating international law. The Chinese consul general in Osaka went further, threatening Takaichi with beheading. China has since canceled airline flights to Japan and banned exports of critical minerals.

In April, the Japanese destroyer Ikazuchi passed through the Taiwan Strait en route to the Philippines-based Balikatan exercise — deliberately on the anniversary of the 1895 treaty that forced China to cede Taiwan to Japan.

Beyond Defense: A New Pacific Player

Japan's ambitions extend well beyond spending. Tokyo has eased its long-running ban on arms exports, agreeing to sell six decommissioned destroyers to the Philippines and more modern frigates to Australia and potentially New Zealand. Last week, Japan signed a $1 billion partnership with Washington on quantum computing, fusion energy, biotechnology, and particle physics.

A July 2026 Congressional Research Service report to Congress described Takaichi as "accelerating" Japan's security normalization, noting that Tokyo had upgraded intelligence capabilities, removed restrictions on arms transfers, and expanded cooperation with regional partners.

The February election gave Takaichi's coalition a supermajority — enough to amend Japan's pacifist post-war constitution, drafted under Allied occupation, which officially bars Tokyo from maintaining a military with "war potential."

Beijing Sharpens Its Response

China's military publications have taken an increasingly anti-Japanese tone. The People's Liberation Army Daily noted that Japan's declared plutonium stockpile of 44 metric tons could theoretically produce 5,500 atomic warheads. Chinese coastguard vessels have become an almost constant presence near the disputed Senkaku islands over the past 18 months.

A RAND Corporation analysis published in March argued Japan should privately commit to helping sink a Chinese invasion fleet headed for Taiwan, calling it "a commitment to the U.S.-Japan alliance — and to Japan's own survival."

For the Indo-Pacific region, the trajectory is clear: Japan is no longer content to be America's quiet junior partner. Whether that leads to greater deterrence or a more dangerous spiral with China is the central security question of the decade.
image_caption: Japan's Self-Defense Forces have expanded joint operations with the United States across the Pacific. Tokyo has boosted defense spending past $58 billion under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
nri_angle: Japan's military transformation has significant implications for the Indian diaspora in the Asia-Pacific, as Tokyo's deepening security partnerships reshape the regional order that affects trade, travel, and strategic stability across the Indo-Pacific.
author: Diaspora Desk
